scenario: Today's recommendation and ads track has two threads. The first is where training signals come from: Meta uses auxiliary signals such as pre-click viewing time and add-to-cart events to fill in rare conversion labels, and another paper uses behavior patterns learned from popular items to correct the content embeddings of long-tail items. The second is the details around launch. How to encode numerical features has to be re-tested on your own data, and whether a click opens a website or an app is worth deciding click by click. Headline rewrites by LLMs that push up rankings now also have a defense with no added latency.

papers.title: Numerical Embeddings for CTR Prediction: A Taxonomy, Unified Benchmark, and Open-Source FuxiCTR Extension
papers.authors: Heng Yao, Hanwei Zhu, Tianying Liu, Yulou Shu, Siyun Hou
papers.abstract: Numerical embeddings map scalar features into vectors before a click-through rate (CTR) backbone combines the fields. To our knowledge, NumEmbBench is the first open benchmark dedicated to comparing numerical embeddings for CTR prediction. We classify 18 configurations into six mechanism-based families and evaluate them through one FuxiCTR interface. After equal-budget validation tuning, we compare frozen configurations on three datasets, nine backbones, and five seeds under a shared train-only z-score protocol. DEER has the best mean rank, but six methods lead at least one dataset--backbone setting. A matched native-scale test changes the winner in 11 of 27 settings, while paired latency measurements show that accuracy and inference cost need not move together. Code and per-seed results: https://github.com/YH-learning/NumEmbBench
papers.summary: There are a dozen or so ways for a CTR model to turn numerical features such as prices and counts into vectors, and in one fair comparison no single method wins everywhere. This used to be hard to compare, because papers differ in preprocessing and training pipelines. This paper puts 18 of them into one codebase with the same tuning budget and compares them across several datasets and backbones. DEER has the best overall rank, but it does not win everywhere: change the dataset or the backbone and the leader can change. When the inputs switch from standardized values back to their original scale, the winner changes in 11 of 27 settings. Accuracy and inference latency also do not rise and fall together. So how to encode numerical features has to be re-tested on your own data and backbone.

papers.title: Improving Ads Ranking Models with Auxiliary Supervision: Techniques and Insights
papers.authors: Nikhil Bhale, Apurva Pathak, SaiSujithKumarReddy MarapaReddy, Xiao Yin, Prateek Bhansali
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of post-click Conversion Rate (CVR) is essential for personalized ad delivery in the advertising industry. Traditional ads ranking models rely on conversion events (e.g., a user purchasing an item) as ground truth labels for training. However, these conversion events are often sparse or missing, which limits the effectiveness of model learning. The primary contributions of this paper are: (1) a case study on the use of auxiliary supervision from a diverse set of user events and metadata signals beyond traditional conversion events, and (2) advanced modeling techniques designed to maximize the value of these signals. We detail architectural innovations such as linearized labels for improved auxiliary signal precision, a split architecture to facilitate training task decomposition, and a novel Label Combination (LaCo) approach for robustly managing noisy auxiliary data. Empirical results demonstrate that these methods deliver measurable improvements in ranking models,
papers.summary: Ad CVR models are trained on conversion events such as purchases and installs, but conversions are rare, and about half of the training samples in this Meta model have no conversion label. The paper fills the gap with other signals: how long a user looked at the ad before clicking, add-to-cart events, the semantics of the ad content and similar signals all become auxiliary tasks trained alongside the main task, at no extra online inference cost. Auxiliary signals are often noisy. The most effective fix is called LaCo, and it works on yes-or-no signals, such as whether the user added the item to the cart. LaCo combines several such signals with AND, OR and XOR, picks the combination that best matches real conversions, above all the one with the fewest false positives, and trains on it as a new label. It lowers offline NE by 0.25%. After these changes shipped together with other improvements, advertiser conversion volume rose with statistical significance in A/B tests. For teams doing conversion prediction, making auxiliary labels accurate pays off more than piling on more auxiliary tasks.

papers.title: PACT: Defending Recommendation against Promotional News Rewriting via Attack-Diverse Score Consistency
papers.authors: Chongxian Chen, Fan Mo, Xin Fan, Hayato Yamana
papers.abstract: Personalized news recommenders are increasingly vulnerable to LLM-powered promotional attacks, where content providers rephrase headlines to manipulate rankings without altering underlying facts. Defending against such manipulation requires covering a wide spectrum of LLM generators and optimization strategies--ranging from stylistic prompting to reinforcement feedback--without incurring prohibitive training or inference costs. In this work, we present PACT (Pooled Attack Consistency Training), a model-agnostic defense that decouples relevance estimation from superficial rhetorical variations. PACT integrates three synergistic operations: it pools offline, fact-checked rewrites from multi-generator and multi-strategy attack sources; samples a constant number of variants at each training visit to yield an unbiased estimator of the pool-wide consistency objective under a fixed compute budget; and aligns original and rewritten ranking scores within the same user context jointly with click
papers.summary: A news publisher can ask an LLM to make a headline more eye-catching without changing a single fact, and the ranking still goes up. This paper's defense is called PACT, and it changes only training. Before training, many different LLMs and rewriting methods produce a batch of rewritten headlines for each training article. During training, each time an article comes up, one rewrite is drawn at random, and the model is asked to give the original and the rewritten headline about the same score for the same user. The deployed model keeps its architecture, with no filtering and no added latency. Against the strongest rewriting attack, LANCE, the share of user and article pairs pushed up the ranking on NRMS drops from 61.4% to 55.4%: the attack is weakened, not removed.

papers.title: Auditing Representation-Space Fraud Detection: A Bayesian IRL Framework for Calibrated Uncertainty and Its Limits
papers.authors: Shivam Swarup, Divya Prakash Shrivastava, Rakesh Thakur
papers.abstract: Shilling detectors for recommender systems are almost always evaluated by one number, detection AUROC, with no account of when it can be trusted. We audit representation-space detection with VEIL (Variational Evaluation via Inverse-reinforcement Learning), a pairwise (Bradley-Terry) Bayesian reward-inference framework over frozen encoder embeddings, following the Bayesian auditing paradigm for LLM alignment [1]: (A) a base posterior; (B) a hierarchical ARD extension with learned confidence; and (C) a label-routed organic/attacker mixture used as an evidence-accumulation check.We prove (Proposition 1) that no detector built on a representation invariant to a transformation of user profiles can outperform chance against an attack that is indistinguishable from organic profiles under that invariance.Detection is near-perfect against synthetic-structure attacks (AUROC 0.936-1.000) but collapses under donor-mimicry, which clones a real user's item set and splices in 1-3 target items. Perfor
papers.summary: Papers on detecting fake shilling accounts in recommender systems usually report a single AUROC. This paper finds that detectors built on model embeddings fail completely under a more realistic attack: the attacker copies a real user's entire item history and slips in only one to three items to promote. On MovieLens-1M, every embedding-based detection score drops to chance. The simplest method works instead: use Jaccard similarity to measure how close each account's item set is to its most similar other account, and AUROC reaches above 0.92. The cause lies in the representation itself. LightGCN's embeddings place a fake account close to the real user it copied, which erases the signal that separates them. So any learned detector should be paired with a similarity check that looks directly at the raw records.

papers.title: Dynamic Click Destinations: Personalizing Post Ad-Click Landing Experiences
papers.authors: Apurva Pathak, Yuya Shiraki, Iman Jenabzadeh, Nikhil Bhale, Yuwen Tan, Shashank Rangarajan, Amirmehdi Sharifzad
papers.abstract: Apps that monetize outbound (offsite) ad clicks have multiple post ad-click levers that influence user and business outcomes, including the landing page shown on the advertiser's site, whether the click resolves to a webpage or an app on the user's device, and whether it resolves to a native in-product surface or an external website. We refer to personalization over these levers as post ad-click destination automation. The optimal destination is heterogeneous across users, advertisers, placements, devices, and inferred intent, making static, one-size-fits-all destination policies suboptimal. We present Dynamic Click Destinations (DCD), a production personalization framework that selects a destination for each eligible offsite ad click to maximize Advertiser Value (AV), a value-weighted conversion outcome. DCD applies to any post-click destination decision where the system can choose among destination options at click time and downstream conversion feedback is available. We describe an
papers.summary: A user taps an offsite ad: should it open the advertiser's website, or jump straight into the advertiser's app already installed on the phone? Switching the default from web to app for everyone actually lowers overall advertiser value (value-weighted conversions) by 1.05%, with a small gain only on ads optimizing for purchases. In other words, which destination is better depends on each click. This paper from Meta picks the destination for each click separately, and the model went through three generations. The last one directly predicts which of the two destinations is better, with training labels taken from the difference between a larger model's conversion scores for the two destinations. In online A/B tests, this generation raises advertiser value by 0.54% over always opening the website. Where a click sends the user is an often overlooked lever for optimization.

papers.title: Efficient Conformal Calibration for Paired Recommendation Decisions
papers.authors: Xinyu Qiao, Yichen Lin, Zhewen Chen, Xue Wang, Tao Yao
papers.abstract: Risk control can suppress useful changes to a frozen recommendation rule. We study how to recover valid activation from the same observed fractional losses. Two specified internal calibrators can lose efficiency by compressing losses into their sum or clipping auxiliary inverse counts before averaging. We propose Averaged Conformal Risk Calibration, or ACRC, which averages before clipping. A product identity proves expected-risk validity, while pointwise bounds characterize the additional activation. For fixed populations sampled without replacement, we connect activation to signed utility under heterogeneous users and switching constraints. Near the budgets, positive population mean gain and the stated nondegeneracy conditions give positive leading-order utility increments despite sampling dependence. Across six datasets, changing only calibration improves discounted net utility by $0.010226$ over raw and $0.008337$ over RB. A separately frozen Jester confirmation gives $0.011025 \pm
papers.summary: A post-processing rule on a trained recommender, such as swapping a few items or reordering, may improve the average result but hurt some users. The usual safeguard is conformal risk control: use held-out data to set a threshold that keeps the expected loss within a budget. But it is often too conservative and blocks useful changes too. This paper finds the problem is wasted information during calibration. One existing method only records whether each user got worse, so a slight drop counts the same as a severe one. The paper's calibration method (ACRC) charges the budget by the actual size of each loss, so a slight drop uses only a little budget, and more changes get through under the same risk guarantee. On 6 datasets, changing only this calibration step gives higher net utility than the existing calibration methods.

papers.title: Yielding Fairness: Coupled Learning and Fairness for Value-Weighted Ranking
papers.authors: Ami Tavory, Yaniv Sheena, Shaked Bar, Yair Zagdansky
papers.abstract: Risk screening and recommendation systems pass or block accounts that generate both value and loss. Under a blocked-value budget, a cap on expected value forgone through blocking, the optimal ranking orders accounts by expected value per unit expected loss, a ratio of conditional expectations. This rule can conflict with accepted harm or net-harm criteria, blocking accounts that another criterion would pass at the same budget. We call these cases account-level objections and define group complaint disparity as the difference between groups' normalized realized objections. Weighted binary cross-entropy (W-BCE) implements the value-per-loss order with one score. Objection penalties modify the ranking, while group multipliers scale those penalties differently by group, tracing tradeoffs between loss capture and complaint disparity. This preserves the value-budgeted ranking structure and makes the cost of reducing contestable blocks explicit. Across public recommendation, insurance, credit
papers.summary: Risk screening and recommendation systems often decide whether to pass or block an account, and an account brings both value and loss. If the value lost by blocking has a cap, the best ranking orders accounts by how much value each unit of expected loss carries, blocking the lowest ratio first until the value budget is used up. Another common criterion blocks by expected loss (or loss minus value), from largest to smallest. Under the same budget, the ratio rule may block an account this criterion would pass, and the paper counts this as a contestable block. When training the ranking score, the paper adds a penalty for accounts that would trigger such a block, and the heavier the penalty, the more the account is pushed toward the pass side. Using different penalty multipliers for different groups traces a trade-off curve between how much loss is caught and the gap in complaints between groups. On public recommendation, insurance and credit data, group-specific penalties narrowed the gap in some groups, but on average they were not significantly better than group-blind penalties.

papers.title: PACERec: Progressive Adaptation of LLM Item Embeddings with Collaborative Evidence for Recommendation
papers.authors: Junzhao Huang, Xi Wu, Zihan Wang, Zijing Wang, Ming Wang, Kang Liu, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng, Daling Wang, Yifei Zhang, Ting Yang, Xurui Li
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) embeddings have been increasingly adopted in sequential recommendation to encode static item attributes and alleviate the limitations of item ID embeddings under sparse interactions. However, these embeddings typically capture only static content similarity while neglecting sequential transitions, and since their adaptation quality relies on sparse per-item updates or global geometric calibration, existing methods still struggle to explicitly transfer preceding interaction contexts from frequent to long-tail items under unevenly distributed behavioral evidence, limiting recommendation effectiveness across the catalog. To address this challenge, we propose PACERec, an ID-free progressive adaptation framework that incorporates preceding interaction contexts into semantic representation adaptation by learning a shared velocity field from items with sufficient interactions via frequency-weighted flow matching. In this way, PACERec progressively guides static LLM
papers.summary: Sequential recommenders often use LLM item embeddings to help long-tail items, but these embeddings only capture whether item contents are similar, not what users tend to view right after what. Long-tail items have too little behavior data to correct their embeddings on their own. PACERec first computes a behavioral target for each item: it takes the items users viewed just before choosing it and computes a weighted average of their content embeddings, with more recent items weighted higher. The model then learns one correction pattern shared by all items: given where a vector is now, it computes which direction to move next and by how much, moving the content embedding step by step toward the behavioral target. This pattern is learned mainly from popular items, whose behavioral targets are reliable. A long-tail item only needs its content embedding to use it directly. On three datasets and three sequential models, tail-item NDCG@10 is on average 33.31% higher than the strongest baseline in each setting.

papers.title: RecRSI: Mechanism-Guided Discovery of Recommendation Algorithms
papers.authors: Tingran Gan, Zhouziyue Lu, Dian Jin, Tao Li, Yang Gao, Ming Liu, Weiwen Liu, Jianghao Lin, Weinan Zhang, Yong Yu
papers.abstract: Improving recommendation algorithms for the Web requires coordinating interacting design choices and learning from experiments. We present RecRSI, an LLM-based research framework that uses mechanism hypotheses to organize algorithm discovery. Each hypothesis links a proposed mechanism change to a reference design, a rationale, and an expected observation. MechSpace derives implementable primitives and composition rules from the task source; Research Line uses this space and prior evidence to develop and test hypotheses; Mechanism Feedback carries outcomes and their design context into subsequent research. This organization makes each experiment inform which mechanisms to develop, revise, or combine next. Across four initial recommenders and four datasets, RecRSI yields average relative improvements of 8.48% in NDCG@5 and 6.88% in HR@5 over the initial algorithms, and 2.60% and 2.20%, respectively, over the strongest competing result for each setting and metric. Component and process st
papers.summary: When an LLM agent tries to improve recommendation algorithms automatically, the hard part is that one experiment's result rarely tells it what to change next. RecRSI attaches a mechanism hypothesis to every change: which component to modify, which existing design it draws on, why it should work, and what result to expect. After the experiment, the result and its design context are passed on to later research and used to decide which mechanisms to develop, revise or combine next. Across several initial recommenders and datasets, it raises NDCG@5 by 8.48% on average relative to the initial algorithms, and by 2.60% over the strongest competing method in each setting. This shows that automated algorithm work keeps improving only when each experiment leaves a reusable conclusion.

papers.title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale
papers.authors: Xiaohe Dong, Jonathan He, Jesus Francisco Anaya Gonzalez, Purbesh Sahoo, Daniel Wang
papers.abstract:
Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020.  F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that [...]

Read More...

The post F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
papers.summary: The more than twenty thousand features used in Meta ads ranking used to be released together, so a single broken feature definition stopped every feature from shipping. They were tied together because they were compiled into one merged computation graph, which let shared computation run only once. F3 Lightning turns each feature into a unit that can be compiled, validated, deployed and rolled back on its own, while keeping the shared computation. It does this by giving each shared step a stable identifier, and all features share one execution plan and one block of memory. As a result, comparable features reach production about 3.6 times faster, with no increase in compute cost. Faster feature releases mean more model iterations in the same amount of time.
